entries.a38e836df5aeb5f288e4498db22e9a66e3fab940: <div sID="gen33441" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="1Pet.3" sID="1Pet.3"/> <div eID="gen33441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33442" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33443" type="x-p"/> Wherein the apostle describes the duties of husbands and wives one to another, beginning with the duty of the wife, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.1-1Pet.3.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. He exhorts Christians to unity, love, compassion, peace, and patience under sufferings; to oppose the slanders of their enemies, not by returning evil for evil, or railing for railing, but by blessing; by a ready account of their faith and hope, and by keeping a good conscience, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.8-1Pet.3.17">ver. 8-17</reference>. To encourage them to this, he proposes the example of Christ, who suffered, the just for the unjust, but yet punished the old world for their disobedience, and saved the few who were faithful in the days of Noah, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.18-1Pet.3.22">ver. 18, to the end</reference>.
entries.d4c221bc84d38a187f4be41511d2d1e921a5c7d9: <div eID="gen33443" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33442" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Duties of Husbands and Wives. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen33444" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Likewise, ye wives, <hi type="italic">be</hi> in subjection to your own husbands; that, if any obey not the word, they also may without the word be won by the conversation of the wives; <hi type="super">2</hi> While they behold your chaste conversation <hi type="italic">coupled</hi> with fear. <hi type="super">3</hi> Whose adorning let it not be that outward <hi type="italic">adorning</hi> of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; <hi type="super">4</hi> But <hi type="italic">let it be</hi> the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, <hi type="italic">even the ornament</hi> of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price. <hi type="super">5</hi> For after this manner in the old time the holy women also, who trusted in God, adorned themselves, being in subjection unto their own husbands: <hi type="super">6</hi> Even as Sara obeyed Abraham, calling him lord: whose daughters ye are, as long as ye do well, and are not afraid with any amazement. <hi type="super">7</hi> Likewise, ye husbands, dwell with <hi type="italic">them</hi> according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered. <div eID="gen33444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33445" type="x-p"/> The apostle having treated of the duties of subjects to their sovereigns, and of servants to their masters, proceeds to explain the duty of husbands and wives. <div eID="gen33445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33446" type="x-p"/> I. Lest the Christian matrons should imagine that their conversion to Christ, and their interest in all Christian privileges, exempted them from subjection to their pagan or Jewish husbands, the apostle here tells them, <div eID="gen33446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33447" type="x-p"/> 1. In what the duty of wives consists. <div eID="gen33447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33448" type="x-p"/> (1.) In <hi type="italic">subjection,</hi> or an affectionate submission to the will, and obedience to the just authority, of <hi type="italic">their own husbands,</hi> which obliging conduct would be the most likely way to win those disobedient and unbelieving husbands who had rejected the word, or who attended to no other evidence of the truth of it than what they saw in the prudent, peaceable, and exemplary <hi type="italic">conversation of their wives.</hi> Learn, [1.] Every distinct relation has its particular duties, which ministers ought to preach, and the people ought to understand. [2.] A cheerful <hi type="italic">subjection,</hi> and a loving, reverential respect, are duties which Christian women owe their husbands, whether they be good or bad; these were due from Eve to Adam before the fall, and are still required, though much more difficult now than they were before, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.16">Gen. iii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.11">1 Tim. ii. 11</reference>. [3.] Though the design of the word of the gospel is to win and gain souls to Christ Jesus, yet there are many so obstinate that they will not be <hi type="italic">won by the word.</hi> [4.] There is nothing more powerful, next to the word of God, to win people, than a good conversation, and the careful discharge of relative duties. [5.] Irreligion and infidelity do not dissolve the bonds, nor dispense with the duties, of civil relations; <hi type="italic">the wife</hi> must discharge her duty <hi type="italic">to her own husband,</hi> though he <hi type="italic">obey not the word.</hi> <div eID="gen33448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33449" type="x-p"/> (2.) In <hi type="italic">fear,</hi> or reverence to their husbands, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.33">Eph. v. 33</reference>. <div eID="gen33449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33450" type="x-p"/> (3.) In a <hi type="italic">chaste conversation,</hi> which their unbelieving husbands would accurately observe and attend to. [1.] Evil men are strict observers of the conversation of the professors of religion; their curiosity, envy, and jealousy, make them watch narrowly the ways and lives of good people. [2.] <hi type="italic">A chaste conversation,</hi> attended with due and proper respect to every one, is an excellent means to win them to the faith of the gospel and obedience to the word. <div eID="gen33450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33451" type="x-p"/> (4.) In preferring the ornaments of the mind to those of the body. [1.] He lays down a rule in regard to the dress of religious women, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.3">v. 3</reference>. Here are three sorts of ornaments forbidden: <hi type="italic">plaiting of hair,</hi> which was commonly used in those times by lewd women; <hi type="italic">wearing of gold,</hi> or ornaments made of <hi type="italic">gold,</hi> was practised by Rebecca, and Esther, and other religious women, but afterwards became the attire chiefly of harlots and wicked people; <hi type="italic">putting on of apparel,</hi> which is not absolutely forbidden, but only too much nicety and costliness in it. Learn, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Religious people should take care that all their external behaviour be answerable to their profession of Christianity: <hi type="italic">They must be holy in all manner of conversation. Secondly,</hi> The outward adorning of the body is very often sensual and excessive; for instance, when it is immoderate, and above your degree and station in the world, when you are proud of it and puffed up with it, when you dress with design to allure and tempt others, when your apparel is too rich, curious, or superfluous, when your fashions are fantastical, imitating the levity and vanity of the worst people, and when they are immodest and wanton. The attire of a harlot can never become a chaste Christian matron. [2.] Instead of the outward adorning of the body, he directs Christian wives to put on much more excellent and beautiful ornaments, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.4">v. 4</reference>. Here note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The part to be adorned: <hi type="italic">The hidden man of the heart;</hi> that is, the soul; the hidden, the inner man. Take care to adorn and beautify your souls rather than your bodies. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The ornament prescribed. It must, in general, be something <hi type="italic">not corruptible,</hi> that beautifies the soul, that is, the graces and virtues of God's Holy Spirit. The ornaments of the body are destroyed by the moth, and perish in the using; but the grace of God, the longer we wear it, the brighter and better it is. More especially, the finest ornament of Christian women is <hi type="italic">a meek and quiet spirit,</hi> a tractable easy temper of mind, void of passion, pride, and immoderate anger, discovering itself in a quiet obliging behaviour towards their husbands and families. If the husband be harsh, and averse to religion (which was the case of these good wives to whom the apostle gives this direction), there is no way so likely to win him as a prudent meek behaviour. At least, a quiet spirit will make a good woman easy to herself, which, being visible to others, becomes an amiable ornament to a person in the eyes of the world. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The excellency of it. Meekness and calmness of spirit are, in the sight of God, of great price—amiable in the sight of men, and precious in the sight of God. Learn, 1. A true Christian's chief care lies in the right ordering and commanding of his own spirit. Where the hypocrite's work ends, there the true Christian's work begins. 2. The endowments of the inner man are the chief ornaments of a Christian; but especially a composed, calm, and quiet spirit, renders either man or woman beautiful and lovely. <div eID="gen33451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33452" type="x-p"/> 2. The duties of Christian wives being in their nature difficult, the apostle enforces them by the example, (1.) Of the holy women of old, who trusted in God, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.5">v. 5</reference>. "You can pretend nothing of excuse from the weakness of your sex, but what they might. They lived <hi type="italic">in old time,</hi> and had less knowledge to inform them and fewer examples to encourage them; yet in all ages they practised this duty; they were <hi type="italic">holy women,</hi> and therefore their example is obligatory; they <hi type="italic">trusted in God,</hi> and yet did not neglect their duty to man: the duties imposed upon you, of a quiet spirit and of subjection to your own husbands, are not new, but what have ever been practised by the greatest and best women in the world." (2.) Of Sara, who obeyed her husband, and followed him when he went from Ur of the Chaldeans, <hi type="italic">not knowing whither he went,</hi> and <hi type="italic">called him lord,</hi> thereby showing him reverence and acknowledging his superiority over her; and all this though she was declared a princess by God from heaven, by the change of her name, "<hi type="italic">Whose daughters you are</hi> if you imitate her in faith and good works, and do not, through fear of your husbands, either quit the truth you profess or neglect your duty to them, but readily perform it, without either fear or force, out of conscience towards God and sense of duty to them." Learn, [1.] God takes exact notice, and keeps an exact record, of the actions of all men and women in the world. [2.] The subjection of wives to their husbands is a duty which has been practised universally by holy women in all ages. [3.] The greatest honour of any man or woman lies in a humble and faithful deportment of themselves in the relation or condition in which Providence has placed them. [4.] God takes notice of the good that is in his servants, to their honour and benefit, but covers a multitude of failings; Sara's infidelity and derision are overlooked, when her virtues are celebrated. [5.] Christians ought to do their duty to one another, not out of fear, nor from force, but from a willing mind, and in obedience to the command of God. Wives should be in subjection to their churlish husbands, not from dread and amazement, but from a desire to do well and to please God. <div eID="gen33452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33453" type="x-p"/> II. The husband's duty to the wife comes next to be considered. <div eID="gen33453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33454" type="x-p"/> 1. The particulars are, (1.) <hi type="italic">Cohabitation,</hi> which forbids unnecessary separation, and implies a mutual communication of goods and persons one to another, with delight and concord. (2.) <hi type="italic">Dwelling with the wife according to knowledge;</hi> not according to lust, as brutes; nor according to passion, as devils; but according to knowledge, as wise and sober men, who know the word of God and their own duty. (3.) <hi type="italic">Giving honour to the wife</hi>—giving due respect to her, and maintaining her authority, protecting her person, supporting her credit, delighting in her conversation, affording her a handsome maintenance, and placing a due trust and confidence in her. <div eID="gen33454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33455" type="x-p"/> 2. The reasons are, Because she is <hi type="italic">the weaker vessel</hi> by nature and constitution, and so ought to be defended: but then the wife is, in other and higher respects, equal to her husband; they are <hi type="italic">heirs together of the grace of life,</hi> of all the blessings of this life and another, and therefore should live peaceably and quietly one with another, and, if they do not, their prayers one with another and one for another will be hindered, so that often "you will not pray at all, or, if you do, you will pray with a discomposed ruffled mind, and so without success." Learn, (1.) The weakness of the female sex is no just reason either for separation or contempt, but on the contrary it is a reason for honour and respect: <hi type="italic">Giving honour to the wife as unto the weaker vessel.</hi> (2.) There is an honour due to all who are heirs of the grace of life. (3.) All married people should take care to behave themselves so lovingly and peaceably one to another that they may not by their broils hinder the success of their prayers.
entries.47c89ab9dc579c60259c569f1266cb00e289c85e: <div eID="gen33455" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Duties towards Friends and Enemies. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen33456" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Finally, <hi type="italic">be ye</hi> all of one mind, having compassion one of another, love as brethren, <hi type="italic">be</hi> pitiful, <hi type="italic">be</hi> courteous: <hi type="super">9</hi> Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing. <hi type="super">10</hi> For he that will love life, and see good days, let him refrain his tongue from evil, and his lips that they speak no guile: <hi type="super">11</hi> Let him eschew evil, and do good; let him seek peace, and ensue it. 12 For the eyes of the Lord <hi type="italic">are</hi> over the righteous, and his ears <hi type="italic">are open</hi> unto their prayers: but the face of the Lord <hi type="italic">is</hi> against them that do evil. <hi type="super">13</hi> And who <hi type="italic">is</hi> he that will harm you, if ye be followers of that which is good? <hi type="super">14</hi> But and if ye suffer for righteousness' sake, happy <hi type="italic">are ye:</hi> and be not afraid of their terror, neither be troubled; <hi type="super">15</hi> But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and <hi type="italic">be</hi> ready always to <hi type="italic">give</hi> an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear: <div eID="gen33456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33457" type="x-p"/> The apostle here passes from special to more general exhortations. <div eID="gen33457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33458" type="x-p"/> I. He teaches us how Christians and friends should treat one another. He advises Christians to <hi type="italic">be all of one mind,</hi> to be unanimous in the belief of the same faith, and the practice of the same duties of religion; and, whereas the Christians at that time were many of them in a suffering condition, he charges them to <hi type="italic">have compassion one of another,</hi> to <hi type="italic">love as brethren,</hi> to <hi type="italic">pity</hi> those who were in distress, and to <hi type="italic">be courteous</hi> to all. Hence learn, 1. Christians should endeavour to be all of one mind in the great points of faith, in real affection, and in Christian practice; they should be <hi type="italic">like-minded one to another, according to Christ Jesus</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.5">Rom. xv. 5</reference>), not according to man's pleasure, but God's word. 2. Though Christians cannot be exactly of the same mind, yet they should have compassion one for another, and love as brethren; they ought not to persecute or hate one another, but love one another with more than common affection; they should love as brethren. 3. Christianity requires pity to the distressed, and civility to all. He must be a flagrant sinner, or a vile apostate, who is not a proper object of civil courtesy, <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.11">1 Cor. v. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2John.1.10-2John.1.11">2 John 10, 11</reference>. <div eID="gen33458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33459" type="x-p"/> II. He instructs us how to behave towards enemies. The apostle knew that Christians would <hi type="italic">be hated</hi> and evil-entreated <hi type="italic">of all men for Christ's sake;</hi> therefore, <div eID="gen33459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33460" type="x-p"/> 1. He warns them not to return <hi type="italic">evil for evil, nor railing for railing;</hi> but, on the contrary, "when they rail at you, do you bless them; when they give you evil words, do you give them good ones; for Christ has both by his word and example called you to bless those that curse you, and has settled a blessing on you as your everlasting inheritance, though you were unworthy." To bear evils patiently, and to bless your enemies, is the way to obtain this blessing of God. Learn, (1.) To <hi type="italic">render evil for evil, or railing for railing,</hi> is a sinful unchristian practice; the magistrate may punish <hi type="italic">evil-doers,</hi> and private men may seek a legal remedy when they are wronged; but private revenge by duelling, scolding, or secret mischief, is forbidden <reference osisRef="Prov.20.22">Prov. xx. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.6.27">Luke vi. 27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.12.17">Rom. xii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.15">1 Thess. v. 15</reference>. To rail is to revile another in bitter, fierce, and reproachful terms; but for ministers to rebuke sharply, and to preach earnestly against the sins of the times, is not railing; all the prophets and apostles practised it, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.10">Isa. lvi. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.3">Zeph. iii. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.20.29">Acts xx. 29</reference>. (2.) The laws of Christ oblige us to return blessing for railing. <reference osisRef="Matt.5.44">Matt. v. 44</reference>, "<hi type="italic">Love your enemies, bless those that curse you, do good to those that hate you, and pray for those that persecute you.</hi> You must not justify them in their sin, but you must do for your enemies all that justice requires or charity commands." We must pity, pray for, and love those who rail at us. (3.) A Christian's calling, as it invests him with glorious privileges, so it obliges him to difficult duties. (4.) All the true servants of God shall infallibly inherit a blessing; they have it already in a great degree, but the full possession of it is reserved to another state and world. <div eID="gen33460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33461" type="x-p"/> 2. He gives an excellent prescription for a comfortable happy life in this quarrelsome ill-natured world (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.10">v. 10</reference>): it is quoted from <reference osisRef="Ps.34.12-Ps.34.14">Ps. xxxiv. 12-14</reference>. "If you earnestly desire that your life should be long, and your days peaceable and prosperous, keep your tongue from reviling, evil-speaking, and slandering, and your lips from lying, deceit, and dissimulation. Avoid doing any real damage or hurt to your neighbour, but be ever ready to do good, and to overcome evil with good; seek peace with all men, and pursue it, though it retire from you. This will be the best way to dispose people to speak well of you, and live peaceably with you." Learn, (1.) Good people under the Old and new Testament were obliged to the same moral duties; to <hi type="italic">refrain the tongue from evil, and the lips from guile,</hi> was a duty in David's time as well as now. (2.) It is lawful to consider temporal advantages as motives and encouragements to religion. (3.) The practice of religion, particularly the right government of the tongue, is the best way to make this life comfortable and prosperous; a sincere, inoffensive, discreet tongue, is a singular means to pass us peaceably and comfortably through the world. (4.) The avoiding of evil, and doing of good, is the way to contentment and happiness both here and hereafter. (5.) It is the duty of Christians not only to embrace peace when it is offered, but to seek and pursue it when it is denied: peace with societies, as well as peace with particular persons, in opposition to division and contention, is what is here intended. <div eID="gen33461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33462" type="x-p"/> 3. He shows that Christians need not fear that such patient inoffensive behaviour as is prescribed will invite and encourage the cruelty of their enemies, for God will thereby be engaged on their side: <hi type="italic">For the eyes of the Lord are over the righteous</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.12">v. 12</reference>); he takes special notice of them, exercises a providential constant government over them, and bears a special respect and affection to them. <hi type="italic">His ears are open to their prayers;</hi> so that if any injuries be offered to them they have this remedy, they may complain of it to their heavenly Father, whose ears are always attentive to the prayers of his servants in their distresses, and who will certainly aid them against their unrighteous enemies. <hi type="italic">But the face of the Lord is against those that do evil;</hi> his anger, and displeasure, and revenge, will pursue them; for he is more an enemy to wicked persecutors than men are. Observe, (1.) We must not in all cases adhere to the express words of scripture, but study the sense and meaning of them, otherwise we shall be led into blasphemous errors and absurdities: we must not imagine that God hath eyes, and ears, and face, though these are the express words of the scripture. (2.) God hath a special care and paternal affection towards all his righteous people. (3.) God doth always hear the prayers of the faithful, <reference osisRef="John.4.31">John iv. 31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.5.14">1 John v. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.4.16">Heb. iv. 16</reference>. (4.) Though God is infinitely good, yet he abhors impenitent sinners, and will pour out his wrath upon those that do evil. He will do himself right, and do all the world justice; and his goodness is no obstruction to his doing so. <div eID="gen33462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33463" type="x-p"/> 4. This patient humble behaviour of Christians is further recommended and urged from two considerations:—(1.) This will be the best and surest way to prevent suffering; for <hi type="italic">who is he that will harm you?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.13">v. 13</reference>. This, I suppose, is spoken of Christians in an ordinary condition, not in the heat of persecution. "Ordinarily, there will be but few so diabolical and impious as to harm those who live so innocently and usefully as you do." (2.) This is the way to improve sufferings. "<hi type="italic">If you be followers of that which is good,</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">suffer,</hi> this is suffering for righteousness; sake (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.14">v. 14</reference>), and will be your glory and your happiness, as it entitles you to the blessing promised by Christ" (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.10">Matt. v. 10</reference>); therefore, [1.] "You need not be afraid of any thing they can do to strike you with terror, neither be much troubled nor concerned about the rage or force of your enemies." Learn, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> to follow always that which is good is the best course we can take to keep out of harm's way. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> To suffer for righteousness sake is the honour and happiness of a Christian; to suffer for the cause of truth, a good conscience, or any part of a Christian's duty, is a great honour; the delight of it is greater than the torment, the honour more than the disgrace, and the gain much greater than the loss. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Christians have no reason to be afraid of the threats or rage of any of their enemies. "Your enemies are God's enemies, <hi type="italic">his face is against them,</hi> his power is above them, they are the objects of his curse, and can do nothing to you but by his permission; therefore trouble not yourselves about them." [2.] Instead of terrifying yourselves with the fear of men, be sure to <hi type="italic">sanctify the Lord God in your hearts</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.15">v. 15</reference>); <hi type="italic">let him be your fear, and let him be your dread,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.8.12-Isa.8.13">Isa. viii. 12, 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fear not those that can only kill the body, but fear him that can destroy body and soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.4-Luke.12.5">Luke xii. 4, 5</reference>. We sanctify the Lord God in our hearts when we with sincerity and fervency adore him, when our thoughts of him are awful and reverend, when we rely upon his power, trust to his faithfulness, submit to his wisdom, imitate his holiness, and give him the glory due to his most illustrious perfections. We sanctify God before others when our deportment is such as invites and encourages others to glorify and honour him; both are required, <reference osisRef="Lev.10.3">Lev. x. 3</reference>. "When this principle is laid deeply into your hearts, the next thing, as to men, is to be always ready, that is, able and willing, <hi type="italic">to give an answer,</hi> or make an apology or defence, of the faith you profess, and that <hi type="italic">to every man that asketh a reason of your hope,</hi> what sort of hope you have, or which you suffer such hardships in the world." Learn, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> An awful sense of the divine perfections is the best antidote against the fear of sufferings; did we fear God more, we should certainly fear men less. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The hope and faith of a Christian are defensible against all the world. There may be a good reason given for religion; it is not a fancy but a rational scheme revealed from heaven, suited to all the necessities of miserable sinners, and centering entirely in the glory of God through Jesus Christ. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Every Christian is bound to answer and apologize for the hope that is in him. Christians should have a reason ready for their Christianity, that it may appear they are not actuated either by folly or fancy. This defence may be necessary more than once or twice, so that Christians should be always prepared to make it, either to the magistrate, if he demand it, or to any inquisitive Christian, who desires to know it for his information or improvement. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> These confessions of our faith ought to be made <hi type="italic">with meekness and fear;</hi> apologies for our religion ought to be made with modesty and meekness, in the fear of God, with jealousy over ourselves, and reverence to our superiors.
entries.d32e6a673ca599d849179f5e6697804566e4d4d9: <div eID="gen33463" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Good Conscience and Good Conversation. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen33464" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Having a good conscience; that, whereas they speak evil of you, as of evildoers, they may be ashamed that falsely accuse your good conversation in Christ. <hi type="super">17</hi> For <hi type="italic">it is</hi> better, if the will of God be so, that ye suffer for well doing, than for evil doing. <div eID="gen33464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33465" type="x-p"/> The confession of a Christian's faith cannot credibly be supported but by the two means here specified—<hi type="italic">a good conscience</hi> and a <hi type="italic">good conversation.</hi> conscience is good when it does its office well, when it is kept pure and uncorrupt, and clear from guilt; then it will justify you, though men accuse you. <hi type="italic">A good conversation in Christ</hi> is a holy life, according to the doctrine and example of Christ. "Look well to your conscience, and to your conversation; and then, though men speak evil of you, and falsely accuse you as evil-doers, you will clear yourselves, and bring them to shame. Perhaps you may think it hard to suffer for well-doing, for keeping a good conscience and a good conversation; but be not discouraged, for it is better for you, though worse for your enemies, that you suffer for well-doing than for evil-doing." Learn, 1. The most conscientious persons cannot escape the censures and slanders of evil men; they will speak evil of them, as of evil-doers, and charge them with crimes which their very souls abhor: Christ and his apostles were so used. 2. A good conscience and a good conversation are the best means to secure a good name; these give a solid reputation and a lasting one. 3. False accusation generally turns to the accuser's shame, by discovering at last the accuser's indiscretion, injustice, falsehood, and uncharitableness. 4. It is sometimes the will of God that good people should suffer for well-doing, for their honesty and for their faith. 5. As well-doing sometimes exposes a good man to suffering, so evil-doing will not exempt an evil man from it. The apostle supposes here that a man may suffer for both. If the sufferings of good people for well-doing be so severe, what will the sufferings of wicked people be for evil-doing? It is a sad condition which that person is in upon whom sin and suffering meet together at the same time; sin makes sufferings to be extreme, unprofitable, comfortless, and destructive.
entries.51bd6d979208a1e8ea33d711e6f7a4f53c02281b: <div eID="gen33465" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Sufferings. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen33466" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit: <hi type="super">19</hi> By which also he went and preached unto the spirits in prison; <hi type="super">20</hi> Which sometime were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing, wherein few, that is, eight souls were saved by water. <div eID="gen33466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33467" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The example of Christ is proposed as an argument for patience under sufferings, the strength of which will be discerned if we consider the several points contained in the words; observe therefore, 1. Jesus Christ himself was not exempted from sufferings in this life, though he had no guilt of his own and could have declined all suffering if he had pleased. 2. The reason or meritorious cause of Christ's suffering was the sins of men: <hi type="italic">Christ suffered for sins.</hi> The sufferings of Christ were a true and proper punishment; this punishment was suffered to expiate and to make an atonement for sin; and it extends to all sin. 3. In the case of our Lord's suffering, it was the just that suffered for the unjust; he substituted himself in our room and stead, and bore our iniquities. He that knew no sin suffered instead of those that knew no righteousness. 4. The merit and perfection of Christ's sacrifice were such that for him to suffer once was enough. The legal sacrifices were repeated from day to day, and from year to year; but the sacrifice of Christ, once offered, purgeth away sin, <reference osisRef="Heb.7.27 Heb.9.26 Heb.9.28 Heb.10.10 Heb.10.12 Heb.10.14">Heb. vii. 27; ix. 26, 28; x. 10, 12, 14</reference>. 5. The blessed end or design of our Lord's sufferings was to bring us to God, to reconcile us to God, to give us access to the Father, to render us and our services acceptable, and to bring us to eternal glory, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.13 Eph.2.18 Eph.3.12 Heb.10.21-Heb.10.22">Eph. ii. 13, 18; iii. 12; Heb. x. 21, 22</reference>. 6. The issue and event of Christ's suffering, as to himself, were these, he was put to death in his human nature, but he was quickened and raised again by the Spirit. Now, if Christ was not exempted from sufferings, why should Christians expect it? If he suffered, to expiate sins, why should not we be content when our sufferings are only for trial and correction, but not for expiation? If he, though perfectly just, why should not we, who are all criminals? If he once suffered, and then entered into glory, shall not we be patient under trouble, since it will be but a little time and we shall follow him to glory? If he <hi type="italic">suffered, to bring us to God,</hi> shall not we submit to difficulties, since they are of so much use to quicken us in our return to God, and in the performance of our duty to him? <div eID="gen33467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33468" type="x-p"/> II. The apostle passes from the example of Christ to that of the old world, and sets before the Jews, to whom he wrote, the different event of those who believed and obeyed Christ preaching by Noah, from those that continued disobedient and unbelieving, intimating to the Jews that they were under a like sentence. God would not wait much longer upon them. They had now an offer of mercy; those that accepted of it should be saved, but those who rejected Christ and the gospel should be as certainly destroyed as ever the disobedient in the times of Noah were. <div eID="gen33468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33469" type="x-p"/> 1. For the explication of this we may notice, (1.) The preacher—Christ Jesus, who has interested himself in the affairs of the church and of the world ever since he was first promised to Adam, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Gen. iii. 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">He went,</hi> not by a local motion, but by special operation, as God is frequently said to move, <reference osisRef="Gen.11.5">Gen. xi. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.5.15">Hos. v. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.1.3">Mic. i. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">He went and preached,</hi> by his Spirit striving with them, and inspiring and enabling Enoch and Noah to plead with them, and <hi type="italic">preach righteousness to them,</hi> as <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.5">2 Pet. ii. 5</reference>. (2.) The hearers. Because they were dead and disembodied when the apostle speaks of them, therefore he properly calls them spirits now <hi type="italic">in prison;</hi> not that they were <hi type="italic">in prison when Christ preached to them,</hi> as the vulgar Latin translation and the popish expositors pretend. (3.) The sin of these people: They were <hi type="italic">disobedient,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">rebellious, unpersuadable,</hi> and <hi type="italic">unbelieving,</hi> as the word signifies; this their sin is aggravated from the patience and <hi type="italic">long-suffering of God</hi> (which <hi type="italic">once waited</hi> upon them for 120 years together), <hi type="italic">while Noah was preparing the ark,</hi> and by that, as well as by his preaching, giving them fair warning of what was coming upon them. (4.) The event of all: Their bodies were drowned, and their spirits cast into hell, which is called a prison (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.25">Matt. v. 25</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.4-2Pet.2.5">2 Pet. ii. 4, 5</reference>); but Noah and his family, who believed and were obedient, <hi type="italic">were saved in the ark.</hi> <div eID="gen33469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33470" type="x-p"/> 2. From the whole we learn that, (1.) God takes exact notice of all the means and advantages that people in all ages have had for the salvation of their souls; it is put to the account of the old world that Christ offered them his help, sent his Spirit, gave them fair warning by Noah, and waited a long time for their amendment. (2.) Though the patience of God wait long upon sinners, yet it will expire at last; it is beneath the majesty of the great God always to wait upon man in vain. (3.) The spirits of disobedient sinners, as soon as they are out of their bodies, are committed to the prison of hell, whence there is no redemption. (4.) The way of the most is neither the best, the wisest, nor the safest way to follow: better to follow the eight in the ark than the eight millions drowned by the flood and damned to hell.
entries.eeaa47885dcd31551ecceb48573c7fc273a6a872: <div eID="gen33470" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christian Baptism. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen33471" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> The like figure whereunto <hi type="italic">even</hi> baptism doth also now save us (not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God,) by the resurrection of Jesus Christ: <hi type="super">22</hi> Who is gone into heaven, and is on the right hand of God; angels and authorities and powers being made subject unto him. <div eID="gen33471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33472" type="x-p"/> Noah's salvation in the ark upon the water prefigured the salvation of all good Christians in the church by baptism; that temporal salvation by the ark was a type, the antitype whereunto is the eternal salvation of believers by baptism, to prevent mistakes about which the apostle, <div eID="gen33472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33473" type="x-p"/> I. Declares what he means by saving baptism; not the outward ceremony of washing with water, which, in itself, does no more than put away the filth of the flesh, but it is that baptism wherein there is a faithful answer or restipulation of a resolved good conscience, engaging to believe in, and be entirely devoted to, God, the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, renouncing at the same time the flesh, the world, and the devil. The baptismal covenant, made and kept, will certainly save us. Washing is the visible sign; this is the thing signified. <div eID="gen33473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33474" type="x-p"/> II. The apostle shows that the efficacy of baptism to salvation depends not upon the work done, but upon the resurrection of Christ, which supposes his death, and is the foundation of our faith and hope, to which we are rendered conformable by dying to sin, and rising again to holiness and newness of life. Learn, 1. The sacrament of baptism, rightly received, is a means and a pledge of salvation. <hi type="italic">Baptism now saveth us.</hi> God is pleased to convey his blessings to us in and by his ordinances, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.38">Acts ii. 38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.22.16">xxii. 16</reference>. 2. The external participation of baptism will save no man without an answerable good conscience and conversation. There must be the answer of a good conscience towards God.—<hi type="italic">Obj.</hi> Infants cannot make such an answer, and therefore ought not to be baptized.—<hi type="italic">Answer,</hi> the true circumcision was that of the heart and of the spirit (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.29">Rom. ii. 29</reference>), which children were no more capable of then than our infants are capable of making this answer now; yet they were allowed circumcision at eight days old. The infants of the Christian church therefore may be admitted to the ordinance with as much reason as the infants of the Jewish, unless they are barred from it by some express prohibition of Christ. <div eID="gen33474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33475" type="x-p"/> III. The apostle, having mentioned the death and resurrection of Christ, proceeds to speak of his ascension, and sitting at the right hand of the Father, as a subject fit to be considered by these believers for their comfort in their suffering condition, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.22">v. 22</reference>. If the advancement of Christ was so glorious after his deep humiliation, let not his followers despair, but expect that after these short distresses they shall be advanced to transcendent joy and glory. Learn, 1. Jesus Christ, after he had finished his labours and his sufferings upon earth, ascended triumphantly into heaven, of which see <reference osisRef="Acts.1.9-Acts.1.11">Acts i. 9-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.16.19">Mark xvi. 19</reference>. He went to heaven to receive his own acquired crown and glory (<reference osisRef="John.17.5">John xvii. 5</reference>), to finish that part of his mediatorial work which could not be done on earth, and make intercession for his people, to demonstrate the fulness of his satisfaction, to take possession of heaven for his people, to prepare mansions for them, and to send down the Comforter, which was to be the first-fruits of his intercession, <reference osisRef="John.16.7">John xvi. 7</reference>. 2. Upon his ascension into heaven, Christ is enthroned at the right hand of the Father. His being said to <hi type="italic">sit</hi> there imports absolute rest and cessation from all further troubles and sufferings, and an advancement to the highest personal dignity and sovereign power. 3. Angels, authorities, and powers, are all made subject to Christ Jesus: <hi type="italic">all power in heaven and earth,</hi> to command, to give law, issue orders, and pronounce a final sentence, is committed to Jesus, God-man, which his enemies will find to their everlasting sorrow and confusion, but his servants to their eternal joy and satisfaction.  <chapter eID="1Pet.3"/> <div eID="gen33475" type="x-p"/>

entries.ccd149890f7b34f53f90bf1fd865edc72fd24779: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18778"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <div sID="gen39986" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.1-1Pet.3.22">1Pe 3:1-22</reference>. Relative Duties of Husbands and Wives: Exhortations to Love and Forbearance: Right Conduct under Persecutions for Righteousness' Sake, after Christ's Example, Whose Death Resulted in Quickening to Us through His Being Quickened Again, of Which Baptism Is the Sacramental Seal.<div eID="gen39986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39987" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18778"/><hi type="bold">1. Likewise--</hi>Greek, "In like manner," as "servants" in their sphere; compare the reason of the woman's subjection, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.8-1Cor.11.10">1Co 11:8-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.11-1Tim.2.14">1Ti 2:11-14</reference>.<div eID="gen39987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39988" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">your own--</hi>enforcing the obligation: it is not strangers ye are required to be subject to. Every time that obedience is enjoined upon women to their husbands, the Greek, "idios," "one's own peculiarly," is used, while the wives of men are designated only by heauton, "of themselves." Feeling the need of leaning on one stronger than herself, the wife (especially if joined to an unbeliever) might be tempted, though only spiritually, to enter into that relation with another in which she ought to stand to "her own spouse (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.34">1Co 14:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.35">35</reference>, "Let them ask their own [idious] husbands at home"); an attachment to the person of the teacher might thus spring up, which, without being in the common sense spiritual adultery, would still weaken in its spiritual basis the married relation [Steiger].<div eID="gen39988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39989" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that, if--</hi>Greek, "that even if." Even if you have a husband that obeys not the word (that is, is an unbeliever).<div eID="gen39989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39990" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without the word--</hi>independently of hearing the word preached, the usual way of faith coming. But Bengel, "without word," that is, without direct Gospel discourse of the wives, "they may (literally, in oldest manuscripts, 'shall,' which marks the almost objective certainty of the result) be won" indirectly. "Unspoken acting is more powerful than unperformed speaking" [OECUMENIUS]. "A soul converted is gained to itself, to the pastor, wife, or husband, who sought it, and to Jesus Christ; added to His treasury who thought not His own precious blood too dear to lay out for this gain" [Leighton]. "The discreet wife would choose first of all to persuade her husband to share with her in the things which lead to blessedness; but if this be impossible, let her then alone diligently press after virtue, in all things obeying him so as to do nothing at any time against his will, except in such things as are essential to virtue and salvation" [Clement of Alexandria]. <div eID="gen39990" type="x-p"/>
entries.6bd96b862ac400bfecc34a73491ace2457239259: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18779"/><div sID="gen39991" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18779"/><hi type="bold">2. behold--</hi>on narrowly looking into it, literally, "having closely observed."<div eID="gen39991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39992" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chaste--</hi>pure, spotless, free from all impurity.<div eID="gen39992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39993" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fear--</hi>reverential, towards your husbands. Scrupulously pure, as opposed to the noisy, ambitious character of worldly women. <div eID="gen39993" type="x-p"/>
entries.afae0aaf367a99efdcfda24adf72d99e0e2c31b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18780"/><div sID="gen39994" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18780"/>3. Literally, "To whom let there belong (namely, as their peculiar ornament) not the outward adornment (usual in the sex which first, by the fall, brought in the need of covering, Note, see on <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.5">1Pe 5:5</reference>) of," &c.<div eID="gen39994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39995" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">plaiting--</hi>artificial braiding, in order to attract admiration.<div eID="gen39995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39996" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wearing--</hi>literally, "putting round," namely, the head, as a diadem--the arm, as a bracelet--the finger, as rings.<div eID="gen39996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39997" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">apparel--</hi>showy and costly. "Have the blush of modesty on thy face instead of paint, and moral worth and discretion instead of gold and emeralds" [Melissa]. <div eID="gen39997" type="x-p"/>
entries.f4e7c2c8c46dd1f1d4bd0e103825e8aff7c161d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18781"/><div sID="gen39998" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18781"/><hi type="bold">4. But--</hi>"Rather." The "outward adornment" of jewelry, &c., is forbidden, in so far as woman loves such things, not in so far as she uses them from a sense of propriety, and does not abuse them. Singularity mostly comes from pride and throws needless hindrances to religion in the way of others. Under costly attire there may be a humble mind. "Great is he who uses his earthenware as if it were plate; not less great is he who uses his silver as if it were earthenware" [Seneca in Alford].<div eID="gen39998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39999" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hidden--</hi>inner man, which the Christian instinctively hides from public view.<div eID="gen39999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40000" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the heart--</hi>consisting in the heart regenerated and adorned by the Spirit. This "inner man of the heart" is the subject of the verb "be," <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.3">1Pe 3:3</reference>, Greek: "Of whom let the inner man be," namely, the distinction or adornment.<div eID="gen40000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40001" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in that--</hi>consisting or standing in that as its element.<div eID="gen40001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40002" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not corruptible--</hi>not transitory, nor tainted with corruption, as all earthly adornments.<div eID="gen40002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40003" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">meek and quiet--</hi>meek, not creating disturbances: quiet, bearing with tranquillity the disturbances caused by others. Meek in affections and feelings; quiet in words, countenance, and actions [Bengel].<div eID="gen40003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40004" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the sight of God--</hi>who looks to inward, not merely outward things.<div eID="gen40004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40005" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of great price--</hi>The results of redemption should correspond to its costly price (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.19">1Pe 1:19</reference>). <div eID="gen40005" type="x-p"/>
entries.362bf6f339f387b82965a8285d6fa42115158282: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18782"/><div sID="gen40006" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18782"/><hi type="bold">5. after this manner--</hi>with the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit (compare the portrait of the godly wife, <reference osisRef="Prov.31.10-Prov.31.31">Pr 31:10-31</reference>).<div eID="gen40006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40007" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">trusted--</hi>Greek, "hoped." "Holy" is explained by "hoped in (so as to be 'united to,' Greek) God." Hope in God is the spring of true holiness [Bengel].<div eID="gen40007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40008" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in subjection--</hi>Their ornament consisted in their subordination. Vanity was forbidden (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.3">1Pe 3:3</reference>) as being contrary to female subjection. <div eID="gen40008" type="x-p"/>
entries.c12ada8ea2a186c0fb7676e4aa12d698ffbcf5aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18783"/><div sID="gen40009" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18783"/><hi type="bold">6. Sara--</hi>an example of faith.<div eID="gen40009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40010" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">calling him lord--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.18.12">Ge 18:12</reference>).<div eID="gen40010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40011" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye are--</hi>Greek, "ye have become": "children" of Abraham and Sara by faith, whereas ye were Gentile aliens from the covenant.<div eID="gen40011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40012" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">afraid with any amazement--</hi>Greek, "fluttering alarm," "consternation." Act well, and be not thrown into sudden panic, as weak females are apt to be, by any opposition from without. Bengel translates, "Not afraid OF any fluttering terror coming from without" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.13-1Pet.3.16">1Pe 3:13-16</reference>). So the Septuagint, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.25">Pr 3:25</reference> uses the same Greek word, which Peter probably refers to. Anger assails men; fear, women. You need fear no man in doing what is right: not thrown into fluttering agitation by any sudden outbreak of temper on the part of your unbelieving husbands, while you do well. <div eID="gen40012" type="x-p"/>
entries.46bc396ce024cd6c353a69aabee22b8b89a429ee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18784"/><div sID="gen40013" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18784"/><hi type="bold">7. dwell--</hi>Greek, "dwelling": connected with the verb, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.17">1Pe 2:17</reference>, "Honor all."<div eID="gen40013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40014" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knowledge--</hi>Christian knowledge: appreciating the due relation of the sexes in the design of God, and acting with tenderness and forbearance accordingly: wisely: with wise consideration.<div eID="gen40014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40015" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them ... giving honour to the wife--</hi>translate and punctuate the Greek rather, "dwelling according to knowledge with the female (Greek adjective, qualifying 'vessel'; not as English Version, a noun) as with the weaker vessel (see on <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.4">1Th 4:4</reference>. Both husband and wife are vessels in God's hand, and of God's making, to fulfil His gracious purposes. Both weak, the woman the weaker. The sense of his own weakness, and that she, like himself, is God's vessel and fabric, ought to lead him to act with tender and wise consideration towards her who is the weaker fabric), giving (literally, 'assigning,' 'apportioning') honor as being also (besides being man and wife) heirs together," &c.; or, as the Vatican manuscript reads, as to those who are also (besides being your wives) fellow heirs." (The reason why the man should give honor to the woman is, because God gives honor to both as fellow heirs; compare the same argument, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.9">1Pe 3:9</reference>). He does not take into account the case of an unbelieving wife, as she might yet believe.<div eID="gen40015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40016" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grace of life--</hi>God's gracious gift of life (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.4">1Pe 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.13">13</reference>).<div eID="gen40016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40017" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that your prayers be not hindered--</hi>by dissensions, which prevent united prayer, on which depends the blessing. <div eID="gen40017" type="x-p"/>
entries.5311cfb138b1bc4b9a21fb85d45a53bb9e2e299d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18785"/><div sID="gen40018" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18785"/>8. General summary of relative duty, after having detailed particular duties from <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.18">1Pe 2:18</reference>.<div eID="gen40018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40019" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of one mind--</hi>as to the faith.<div eID="gen40019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40020" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">having compassion one of another--</hi>Greek, "sympathizing" in the joy and sorrow of others.<div eID="gen40020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40021" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">love as brethren--</hi>Greek, "loving the brethren."<div eID="gen40021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40022" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pitiful--</hi>towards the afflicted.<div eID="gen40022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40023" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">courteous--</hi>genuine Christian politeness; not the tinsel of the world's politeness; stamped with unfeigned love on one side, and humility on the other. But the oldest manuscripts read, "humble-minded." It is slightly different from "humble," in that it marks a conscious effort to be truly humble. <div eID="gen40023" type="x-p"/>
entries.792c48d00224c841891ed42e991fe7a8d79a635c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18786"/><div sID="gen40024" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18786"/><hi type="bold">9. evil--</hi>in deed.<div eID="gen40024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40025" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">railing--</hi>in word.<div eID="gen40025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40026" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blessing--</hi>your revilers; participle, not a noun after "rendering."<div eID="gen40026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40027" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knowing that--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read merely, "because."<div eID="gen40027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40028" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are--</hi>Greek, "were called."<div eID="gen40028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40029" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">inherit a blessing--</hi>not only passive, but also active; receiving spiritual blessing from God by faith, and in your turn blessing others from love [Gerhard in Alford]. "It is not in order to inherit a blessing that we must bless, but because our portion is blessing." No railing can injure you (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.13">1Pe 3:13</reference>). Imitate God who "blesses" you. The first fruits of His blessing for eternity are enjoyed by the righteous even now (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.10">1Pe 3:10</reference>) [Bengel]. <div eID="gen40029" type="x-p"/>
entries.e75c8178ad611059405f201909f4f18eef43a2e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18787"/><div sID="gen40030" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18787"/><hi type="bold">10. will love--</hi>Greek, "wishes to love." He who loves life (present and eternal), and desires to continue to do so, not involving himself in troubles which will make this life a burden, and cause him to forfeit eternal life. Peter confirms his exhortation, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.9">1Pe 3:9</reference>, by <reference osisRef="Ps.34.12-Ps.34.16">Psa 34:12-16</reference>.<div eID="gen40030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40031" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">refrain--</hi>curb, literally, "cause to cease"; implying that our natural inclination and custom is to speak evil. "Men commonly think that they would be exposed to the wantonness of their enemies if they did not strenuously vindicate their rights. But the Spirit promises a life of blessedness to none but those who are gentle and patient of evils" [Calvin].<div eID="gen40031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40032" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">evil ... guile--</hi>First he warns against sins of the tongue, evil-speaking, and deceitful, double-tongued speaking; next, against acts of injury to one's neighbor. <div eID="gen40032" type="x-p"/>
entries.5662130c5b2acc0501e6971a0add62e0faa4a084: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18788"/><div sID="gen40033" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18788"/>11. In oldest manuscripts, Greek, "Moreover (besides his words, in acts), let him."<div eID="gen40033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40034" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eschew--</hi>"turn from."<div eID="gen40034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40035" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ensue--</hi>pursue as a thing hard to attain, and that flees from one in this troublesome world. <div eID="gen40035" type="x-p"/>
entries.7c30cc1a11326cc386f5c0764cae675262c2ead7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18789"/><div sID="gen40036" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18789"/>12. Ground of the promised present and eternal life of blessedness to the meek (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.10">1Pe 3:10</reference>). The Lord's eyes are ever over them for good.<div eID="gen40036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40037" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ears ... unto their prayers--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1John.5.14">1Jo 5:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.5.15">15</reference>).<div eID="gen40037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40038" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">face ... against--</hi>The eyes imply favorable regard; the face of the Lord upon (not as English Version, "against") them that do evil, implies that He narrowly observes them, so as not to let them really and lastingly hurt His people (compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.13">1Pe 3:13</reference>). <div eID="gen40038" type="x-p"/>
entries.36c5d56a34e898ed750a87bb75486dbc5dbad186: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18790"/><div sID="gen40039" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18790"/><hi type="bold">13. who ... will harm you--</hi>This fearless confidence in God's protection from harm, Christ, the Head, in His sufferings realized; so His members.<div eID="gen40039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40040" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if ye be--</hi>Greek, "if ye have become."<div eID="gen40040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40041" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">followers--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read "emulous," "zealous of" (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.14">Tit 2:14</reference>).<div eID="gen40041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40042" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">good--</hi>The contrast in Greek is, "Who will do you evil, if ye be zealous of good?" <div eID="gen40042" type="x-p"/>
entries.a28bc7672a25430a9bcc4e4b149bd0a6ce8d751a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18791"/><div sID="gen40043" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18791"/><hi type="bold">14. But and if--</hi>"But if even." "The promises of this life extend only so far as it is expedient for us that they should be fulfilled" [Calvin]. So he proceeds to state the exceptions to the promise (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.10">1Pe 3:10</reference>), and how the truly wise will behave in such exceptional cases. "If ye should suffer"; if it should so happen; "suffer," a milder word than harm.<div eID="gen40043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40044" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for righteousness--</hi>"not the suffering, but the cause for which one suffers, makes the martyr" [Augustine].<div eID="gen40044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40045" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">happy--</hi>Not even can suffering take away your blessedness, but rather promotes it.<div eID="gen40045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40046" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and--</hi>Greek, "but." Do not impair your blessing (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.9">1Pe 3:9</reference>) by fearing man's terror in your times of adversity. Literally, "Be not terrified with their terror," that is, with that which they try to strike into you, and which strikes themselves when in adversity. This verse and <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.15">1Pe 3:15</reference> is quoted from <reference osisRef="Isa.8.12">Is 8:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.13">13</reference>. God alone is to be feared; he that fears God has none else to fear.<div eID="gen40046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40047" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither be troubled--</hi>the threat of the law, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.36">Le 26:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.65">De 28:65</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.66">66</reference>; in contrast to which the Gospel gives the believer a heart assured of God's favor, and therefore unruffled, amidst all adversities. Not only be not afraid, but be not even agitated. <div eID="gen40047" type="x-p"/>
entries.417cf97715afa5074fcb56637e14fcf16998cbfb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18792"/><div sID="gen40048" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18792"/><hi type="bold">15. sanctify--</hi>hallow; honor as holy, enshrining Him in your hearts. So in the Lord's Prayer, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.9">Mt 6:9</reference>. God's holiness is thus glorified in our hearts as the dwelling-place of His Spirit.<div eID="gen40048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40049" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord God--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read "Christ." Translate, "Sanctify Christ as Lord."<div eID="gen40049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40050" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and--</hi>Greek, "but," or "moreover." Besides this inward sanctification of God in the heart, be also ready always to give, &c.<div eID="gen40050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40051" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">answer--</hi>an apologetic answer defending your faith.<div eID="gen40051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40052" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to every man that asketh you--</hi>The last words limit the universality of the "always"; not to a roller, but to everyone among the heathen who inquires honestly.<div eID="gen40052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40053" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a reason--</hi>a reasonable account. This refutes Rome's dogma, "I believe it, because the Church believes it." Credulity is believing without evidence; faith is believing on evidence. There is no repose for reason itself but in faith. This verse does not impose an obligation to bring forward a learned proof and logical defense of revelation. But as believers deny themselves, crucify the world, and brave persecution, they must be buoyed up by some strong "hope"; men of the world, having no such hope themselves, are moved by curiosity to ask the secret of this hope; the believer must be ready to give an experimental account "how this hope arose in him, what it contains, and on what it rests" [Steiger].<div eID="gen40053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40054" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "but with." Be ready, but with "meekness." Not pertly and arrogantly.<div eID="gen40054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40055" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">meekness--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.4">1Pe 3:4</reference>). The most effective way; not self-sufficient impetuosity.<div eID="gen40055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40056" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fear--</hi>due respect towards man, and reverence towards God, remembering His cause does not need man's hot temper to uphold it. <div eID="gen40056" type="x-p"/>
entries.8dd197c2f0bf0bbebf84244eb444d1a8b989dadd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18793"/><div sID="gen40057" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18793"/><hi type="bold">16. Having a good conscience--</hi>the secret spring of readiness to give account of our hope. So hope and good conscience go together in <reference osisRef="Acts.24.15">Ac 24:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.24.16">16</reference>. Profession without practice has no weight. But those who have a good conscience can afford to give an account of their hope "with meekness."<div eID="gen40057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40058" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whereas--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.12">1Pe 2:12</reference>).<div eID="gen40058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40059" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they speak evil of you, as of evildoers--</hi>One oldest manuscript reads, "ye are spoken against," omitting the rest.<div eID="gen40059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40060" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">falsely accuse--</hi>"calumniate"; the Greek expresses malice shown in deeds as well as in words. It is translated, "despitefully use," <reference osisRef="Matt.5.44">Mt 5:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.6.28">Lu 6:28</reference>.<div eID="gen40060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40061" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">conversation--</hi>life, conduct.<div eID="gen40061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40062" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Christ--</hi>who is the very element of your life as Christians. "In Christ" defines "good." It is your good walk as Christians, not as citizens, that calls forth malice (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.4">1Pe 4:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.14">5, 14</reference>). <div eID="gen40062" type="x-p"/>
entries.1a5c2391bad32b0a68a18ef35524572aa748e702: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18794"/><div sID="gen40063" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18794"/><hi type="bold">17. better--</hi>One may object, I would not bear it so ill if I had deserved it. Peter replies, it is better that you did not deserve it, in order that doing well and yet being spoken against, you may prove yourself a true Christian [Gerhard].<div eID="gen40063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40064" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if the will of God be so--</hi>rather as the optative is in the oldest manuscripts, "if the will of God should will it so." Those who honor God's will as their highest law (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.15">1Pe 2:15</reference>) have the comfort to know that suffering is God's appointment (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.19">1Pe 4:19</reference>). So Christ Himself; our inclination does not wish it. <div eID="gen40064" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b93d0a8a00f5048db4b9b0628b6a9058f77ce7b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18795"/><div sID="gen40065" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18795"/>18. Confirmation of <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.17">1Pe 3:17</reference>, by the glorious results of Christ's suffering innocently.<div eID="gen40065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40066" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">For--</hi>"Because." That is "better," <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.17">1Pe 3:17</reference>, means of which we are rendered more like to Christ in death and in life; for His death brought the best issue to Himself and to us [Bengel].<div eID="gen40066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40067" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Christ--</hi>the Anointed Holy One of God; the Holy suffered for sins, the Just for the unjust.<div eID="gen40067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40068" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">also--</hi>as well as yourselves (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.17">1Pe 3:17</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.21">1Pe 2:21</reference>; there His suffering was brought forward as an example to us; here, as a proof of the blessedness of suffering for well-doing.<div eID="gen40068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40069" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">once--</hi>for all; never again to suffer. It is "better" for us also once to suffer with Christ, than for ever without Christ We now are suffering our "once"; it will soon be a thing of the past; a bright consolation to the tried.<div eID="gen40069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40070" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for sins--</hi>as though He had Himself committed them. He exposed Himself to death by His "confession," even as we are called on to "give an answer to him that asketh a reason of our hope." This was "well-doing" in its highest manifestation. As He suffered, "The Just," so we ought willingly to suffer, for righteousness' sake (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.14">1Pe 3:14</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.12">1Pe 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.17">17</reference>).<div eID="gen40070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40071" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that he might bring us to God--</hi>together with Himself in His ascension to the right hand of God (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.22">1Pe 3:22</reference>). He brings us, "the unjust," justified together with Him into heaven. So the result of Christ's death is His drawing men to Him; spiritually now, in our having access into the Holiest, opened by Christ's ascension; literally hereafter. "Bring us," moreover, by the same steps of humiliation and exaltation through which He Himself passed. The several steps of Christ's progress from lowliness to glory are trodden over again by His people in virtue of their oneness with Him (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.1-1Pet.4.3">1Pe 4:1-3</reference>). "To God," is Greek dative (not the preposition and case), implying that God wishes it [Bengel].<div eID="gen40071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40072" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">put to death--</hi>the means of His bringing us to God.<div eID="gen40072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40073" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the flesh--</hi>that is, in respect to the life of flesh and blood.<div eID="gen40073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40074" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">quickened by the Spirit--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit the Greek article. Translate with the preposition "in," as the antithesis to the previous "in the flesh" requires, "IN spirit," that is, in respect to His Spirit. "Put to death" in the former mode of life; "quickened" in the other. Not that His Spirit ever died and was quickened, or made alive again, but whereas He had lived after the manner of mortal men in the flesh, He began to live a spiritual "resurrection" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.21">1Pe 3:21</reference>) life, whereby He has the power to bring us to God. Two ways of explaining <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.18">1Pe 3:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.19">19</reference>, are open to us: (1) "Quickened in Spirit," that is, immediately on His release from the "flesh," the energy of His undying spirit-life was "quickened" by God the Father, into new modes of action, namely, "in the Spirit He went down (as subsequently He went up to heaven, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.22">1Pe 3:22</reference>, the same Greek verb) and heralded [not salvation, as Alford, contrary to Scripture, which everywhere represents man's state, whether saved or lost, after death irreversible. Nor is any mention made of the conversion of the spirits in prison. See on <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.20">1Pe 3:20</reference>. Nor is the phrase here 'preached the Gospel' (evangelizo), but 'heralded' (ekeruxe) or 'preached'; but simply made the announcement of His finished work; so the same Greek in <reference osisRef="Mark.1.45">Mr 1:45</reference>, 'publish,' confirming Enoch and Noah's testimony, and thereby declaring the virtual condemnation of their unbelief, and the salvation of Noah and believers; a sample of the similar opposite effects of the same work on all unbelievers, and believers, respectively; also a consolation to those whom Peter addresses, in their sufferings at the hands of unbelievers; specially selected for the sake of 'baptism,' its 'antitype' (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.21">1Pe 3:21</reference>), which, as a seal, marks believers as separated from the rest of the doomed world] to the spirits (His Spirit speaking to the spirits) in prison (in Hades or Sheol, awaiting the judgment, <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.4">2Pe 2:4</reference>), which were of old disobedient when," &c. (2) The strongest point in favor of (1) is the position of "sometime," that is, of old, connected with "disobedient"; whereas if the preaching or announcing were a thing long past, we should expect "sometime," or of old, to be joined to "went and preached." But this transposition may express that their disobedience preceded His preaching. The Greek participle expresses the reason of His preaching, "inasmuch as they were sometime disobedient" (compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.6">1Pe 4:6</reference>). Also "went" seems to mean a personal going, as in <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.22">1Pe 3:22</reference>, not merely in spirit. But see the answer below. The objections are "quickened" must refer to Christ's body (compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.21">1Pe 3:21</reference>, end), for as His Spirit never ceased to live, it cannot be said to be "quickened." Compare <reference osisRef="John.5.21">Joh 5:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.11">Ro 8:11</reference>, and other passages, where "quicken" is used of the bodily resurrection. Also, not His Spirit, but His soul, went to Hades. His Spirit was commended by Him at death to His Father, and was thereupon "in Paradise." The theory--(1) would thus require that His descent to the spirits in prison should be after His resurrection! Compare <reference osisRef="Eph.4.9">Ep 4:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.10">10</reference>, which makes the descent precede the ascent. Also Scripture elsewhere is silent about such a heralding, though possibly Christ's death had immediate effects on the state of both the godly and the ungodly in Hades: the souls of the godly heretofore in comparative confinement, perhaps then having been, as some Fathers thought, translated to God's immediate and heavenly presence; but this cannot be proved from Scripture. Compare however, <reference osisRef="John.3.13">Joh 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.18">Col 1:18</reference>. Prison is always used in a bad sense in Scripture. "Paradise" and "Abraham's bosom," the abode of good spirits in Old Testament times, are separated by a wide gulf from Hell or Hades, and cannot be called "prison." Compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.2">2Co 12:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.4">4</reference>, where "paradise" and the "third heaven" correspond. Also, why should the antediluvian unbelievers in particular be selected as the objects of His preaching in Hades? Therefore explain: "Quickened in spirit, in which (as distinguished from in person; the words "in which," that is, in spirit, expressly obviating the objection that "went" implies a personal going) He went (in the person of Noah, "a preacher of righteousness," <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.5">2Pe 2:5</reference>: Alford's own Note, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.17">Ep 2:17</reference>, is the best reply to his argument from "went" that a local going to Hades in person is meant. As "He CAME and preached peace" by His Spirit in the apostles and ministers after His death and ascension: so before His incarnation He preached in Spirit through Noah to the antediluvians, <reference osisRef="John.14.18">Joh 14:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.14.28">28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.26.23">Ac 26:23</reference>. "Christ should show," literally, "announce light to the Gentiles") and preached unto the spirits in prison, that is, the antediluvians, whose bodies indeed seemed free, but their spirits were in prison, shut up in the earth as one great condemned cell (exactly parallel to <reference osisRef="Isa.24.22">Is 24:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.23">23</reference> "upon the earth ... they shall be gathered together as prisoners are gathered in the pit, and shall be shut up in the prison," &c. [just as the fallen angels are judicially regarded as "in chains of darkness," though for a time now at large on the earth, 1Pe 2:4], where <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.18">1Pe 3:18</reference> has a plain allusion to the flood, "the windows from on high are open," compare <reference osisRef="Gen.7.11">Ge 7:11</reference>); from this prison the only way of escape was that preached by Christ in Noah. Christ, who in our times came in the flesh, in the days of Noah preached in Spirit by Noah to the spirits then in prison (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Is 61:1</reference>, end, "the Spirit of the Lord God hath sent me to proclaim the opening of the prison to them that are bound"). So in <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1Pe 1:11</reference>, "the Spirit of Christ" is said to have testified in the prophets. As Christ suffered even to death by enemies, and was afterwards quickened in virtue of His "Spirit" (or divine nature, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.3">Ro 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.45">1Co 15:45</reference>), which henceforth acted in its full energy, the first result of which was the raising of His body (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.21">1Pe 3:21</reference>, end) from the prison of the grave and His soul from Hades; so the same Spirit of Christ enabled Noah, amidst reproach and trials, to preach to the disobedient spirits fast bound in wrath. That Spirit in you can enable you also to suffer patiently now, looking for the resurrection deliverance. <div eID="gen40074" type="x-p"/>
entries.6d8a2146a3ae4aaf6a6877e3841fe831840f093c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18796"/><div sID="gen40075" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18796"/><hi type="bold">20. once--</hi>not in the oldest manuscripts.<div eID="gen40075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40076" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when ... the long-suffering of God waited in the days of Noah--</hi>Oldest manuscripts. Greek, "was continuing to wait on" (if haply men in the hundred twenty years of grace would repent) until the end of His waiting came in their death by the flood. This refutes Alford's idea of a second day of grace having been given in Hades. Noah's days are selected, as the ark and the destroying flood answer respectively to "baptism" and the coming destruction of unbelievers by fire.<div eID="gen40076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40077" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">while the ark was a-preparing--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Heb.11.7">He 11:7</reference>).
