It hence follows that we ought carefully to see how men commonly act when we rely on examples, and that we ought not to fear though we may be few in number.<div eID="gen135737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135738" type="x-p"/>But the fanatics, such as Schuencfeldius, absurdly pervert this testimony, while they seek to take away from sacraments all their power and effect. For Peter did not mean here to teach that Christ’s institution is vain and inefficacious, but only to exclude hypocrites from the hope of salvation, who, as far as they can, deprave and corrupt baptism. Moreover, when we speak of sacraments, two things are to be considered, the sign and the thing itself. In baptism the sign is water, but the thing is the washing of the soul by the blood of Christ and the mortifying of the flesh. The institution of Christ includes these two things. Now that the sign appears often inefficacious and fruitless, this happens through the abuse of men, which does not take away the nature of the sacrament. Let us then learn not to tear away the thing signified from the sign. We must at the same time beware of another evil, such as prevails among the Papists; for as they distinguish not as they ought between the thing and the sign, they stop at the outward element, and on that fix their hope of salvation. Therefore the sight of the water takes away their thoughts from the blood of Christ and the power of the Spirit. They do not regard Christ as the only author of all the blessings therein offered to us; they transfer the glory of his death to the water, they tie the secret power of the Spirit to the visible sign.<div eID="gen135738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135739" type="x-p"/>What then ought we to do? Not to separate what has been joined together by the Lord. We ought to acknowledge in baptism a spiritual washing, we ought to embrace therein the testimony of the remission of sin and the pledge of our renovation, and yet so as to leave to Christ his own honor, and also to the Holy Spirit; so that no part of our salvation should be transferred to the sign. Doubtless when Peter, having mentioned baptism, immediately made this exception, that it is not the putting off of the filth of the flesh, he sufficiently shewed that baptism to some is only the outward act, and that the outward sign of itself avails nothing.<div eID="gen135739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135740" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">But the answer of a good conscience</hi> The word <hi type="italic">question, </hi>or <hi type="italic">questioning</hi>, is to be taken here for “answer,” or testimony. Now Peter briefly defines the efficacy and use of baptism, when he calls attention to conscience, and expressly requires that confidence which can sustain the sight of God and can stand before his tribunal. For in these words he teaches us that baptism in its main part is spiritual, and then that it includes the remission of sins and renovation of the old man; for how can there be a good and pure conscience until our old man is reformed, and we be renewed in the righteousness of God? and how can we answer before God, unless we rely on and are sustained by a gratuitous pardon of our sins? In short, Peter intended to set forth the effect of baptism, that no one might glory in a naked and dead sign, as hypocrites are wont to do.<div eID="gen135740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135741" type="x-p"/>But we must notice what follows, <hi type="italic">by the resurrection of Jesus Christ</hi> By these words he teaches us that we are not to cleave to the element of water, and that what is thereby typified flows from Christ alone, and is to be sought from him. Moreover, by referring to the resurrection, he has regard to the doctrine which he had taught before, that Christ was vivified by the Spirit; for the resurrection was victory over death and the completion of our salvation. We hence learn that the death of Christ is not excluded, but is included in his resurrection. We then cannot otherwise derive benefit from baptism, than by having all our thoughts fixed on the death and the resurrection of Christ.<div eID="gen135741" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Pet.3.21" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen135734" osisID="1Pet.3.21" type="section"/>
entries.ddc68f5045d1aa2a9d3e58514aa691074539e478:
22 Who is on the right hand of God. He recommends to us the ascension of Christ unto heaven, lest our eyes should seek him in the world; and this belongs especially to faith. He commends to our notice his session on the Father’s right hand, lest we should doubt his power to save us. And what his sitting at the right hand of the Father means, we have elsewhere explained, that is, that Christ exercises supreme power everywhere as God’s representative. And an explanation of this is what follows, angels being made subject to him; and he adds powers and authorities only for the sake of amplification, for angels are usually designated by such words. It was then Peter’s object to set forth by these high titles the sovereignty of Christ.
CHAPTER 4
1 Peter 4:1-5
1. Forasmuch then as Christ hath suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves likewise with the same mind: for he that hath suffered in the flesh hath ceased from sin;
1. Christo igitur passo pro nobis carne, vos quoque eadem cogitatione armamini; quod scilicet qui passus est in carne, destitit à peccato;
2. That he no longer should live the rest of his time in the flesh to the lusts of men, but to the will of God.
2. Ne amplius hominum concupiscentiis, sed voluntati Dei, quod residuum est temporis in carne, vivat.
3. For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries:
3. Satis enim nobis est quod anteacto vitae tempore voluntatem gentium patraverimus, quum ambularemus in lasciviis, concupiscentiis, comessationibus, potationibus et nefariis idololatriis:
4. Wherein they think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you:
4. Quod illis videtur insolens, quòd non concurratis in eandem luxus profusionem, ideoque malè loquuntur;
5. Who shall give account to him that is ready to judge the quick and the dead.
5. Qui reddituri sunt rationem ei qui paratus est judicare vivos et mortuos.

               <ns0:p n="1">1 LIkewise <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Eph. 5.22. Col. 3.18. Subjection is required, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 22. and Fear, 33.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Tim. 2.9. Tit. 2.3.</ns0:note> Whose adorning let it not be <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Let it not be chiefly, or not so much the adorning of the outward Man as the inward; the Negative here is to be taken as a comparative, as <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 16.8. and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 14.12. The Apostle doth not absolutely condemn all kind of Ornaments, or rich Attire, which we find used sometimes by the Godly themselves in the Scripture, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 24.22, 30. <ns0:hi>Esth.</ns0:hi> 5.1. compar'd with <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 45.9, 13. where the Spiritual Ornaments of Christ's Spouse are set forth by terms taken from the external Ornaments of <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi>'s Wife, and <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 16.12. these things are spoken of as God's gifts. But he taxeth all vanity, levity, immoderate sumptuousness or luxury in Apparel, and bodily Ornaments in Women (or Men) whatsoever is above their place and condition in the World, or above their estate and ability, such as proceeds from any Lust (Pride, Wantonness, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>) or tends to the provoking or cherishing any, or is accompanied with the neglecting or slighting of inward Beauty, and spiritual Or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />naments.</ns0:note> that outward <ns0:hi>adorning</ns0:hi> of plaiting the hair, or of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 But <ns0:hi>let it be</ns0:hi> the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 45.13. Rom. 2.29.</ns0:note> hidden man of the heart <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The inward Man, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 7.22. and 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.16. either the Soul in opposition to the Body, or the Image of God, and Graces of his Spirit in the Soul, called elsewhere the <ns0:hi>New-Man,</ns0:hi> and opposed to natural corruption or the Old-Man, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 4.24. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3.9, 10.</ns0:note> in that which is not corruptible <ns0:note n="i" place="margin">This relates to what fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lows, <ns0:hi>the Ornament of a meek,</ns0:hi> &c. and is opposed to those external Ornaments before mentioned, which are of a fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ding, perishing nature; whereas this is constant and dura<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble: and therefore Women who are more apt to be over<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />much pleased with external Dresses, and bodily Ornaments, are exhorted rather to enrich and beautify their Souls with Divine Graces, than their Bodies with gawdy Cloaths.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>even the or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nament</ns0:hi> of a meek and quiet Spirit <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">This notes the particular Grace or Graces (parts of the New-Man) in which the Spiritual Beauty and adorning of Womens Souls consists; and either these two words <ns0:hi>meek,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>quiet,</ns0:hi> are but indifferent expressions of the same Grace; or, by <ns0:hi>meekness</ns0:hi> may be meant Gentleness, Easiness and Sweetness of Spirit, in opposition to Moroseness, Fro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wardness, Pride, Passion, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and by <ns0:hi>Quietness,</ns0:hi> a Peaceable, Still, Modest Temper, in opposition to Pragmaticalness, Tal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />kativeness, Clamorousness. These two usually go in con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />junction together, and the latter is the effect of the for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mer; see 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 2.9, 10, 11, 12.</ns0:note> which <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Either this refers to <ns0:hi>Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit,</ns0:hi> or to the whole Sentence, <ns0:hi>the ornament of a meek,</ns0:hi> &c. but the sence is still the same.</ns0:note> is in the sight of God of great price.<ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Who can best judge, (as looking to the inner Man, which is not obvious to the eyes of others) and whose Judgment is most to be valu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed: Here God's Judgment is opposed to the judgement of vain Women, who think to commend themselves to others by outward bravery, and of a vain World which esteems such things.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The excellency of Grace and Spiritual Or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />naments, is set in opposition to Gold and costly Apparel, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> If Women will be fine that they may appear Beauti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful, let them chuse the best Ornaments, those of the Mind and Heart, a meek and quiet Spirit, which are precious in the sight of God himself, rather than these external ones which serve only to draw Men's eyes toward them.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 For after this manner in the old time the holy <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">And therefore worthy of imitation.</ns0:note> women also who trusted <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Whose only hope was in God, and therefore their care to please him.</ns0:note> in God adorned themselves, being in subjection to their own husbands <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> With a meek and quiet Spirit, counting that the best Ornament.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 Even as Sarah <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">After her Name was changed from <ns0:hi>Sarai, my Lady,</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Sarah,</ns0:hi> simply a <ns0:hi>Lady</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Princess,</ns0:hi> because Kings were to come of her, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 17.15, 16. Yet even then she obeyed <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi>; and this is spoken in commendation of her Obedience.</ns0:note> obeyed Abraham <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 18.12.</ns0:note> calling him Lord <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Not meerly in Complement, but in reality, hereby ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />knowledging his Authority and her own Subjection.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="s" place="margin">Not only according to the Flesh, but Spiritually according to the Promise.</ns0:note> whose <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>Children.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> daughters <ns0:hi>t</ns0:hi> ye are <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Either ye are <ns0:hi>made</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>beco<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                        </ns0:gap>e, viz.</ns0:hi> by imitation of her Faith and Holiness, as well as ye are by Kindred and Succession; or, ye are <ns0:hi>declared,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>known</ns0:hi> to be, as the phrase is elsewhere used, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 15.8.</ns0:note> as long as ye do well <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Follow her in good works, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 2.10.</ns0:note>, and are not afraid with any amazement.<ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Or, afraid of any amazement, any thing frightful; or; which might terrify you, taking amazement for the object or cause of Fear, as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 14. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 53.5. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 3.25. and the sence may be, either, so long as ye perform your Duty with a resolute mind, and keep from that which is contrary to your Faith; or, as long as you subject your selves to your Husbands willingly, cheer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fully, and without slavish fear of being losers by your Obe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dience, and faring the worse for your Patience and Sub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mission.</ns0:note>

               <ns0:p n="7">7 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 7.3. Eph. 5.25. Col. 3.19.</ns0:note> Likewise ye husbands dwell <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Perform all Matrimonial Duties to them; by a Synec<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />doche all the duties of that relation are contained under this one of cohabitation.</ns0:note> with them according to knowledg <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Either, according to that knowledg of the Divine Will, which by the Gospel ye have obtain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed; or, prudently and wisely, and as becomes those that understand their Duty.</ns0:note>, giving honour <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Not despising them because of their weakness, or using them as Slaves, but respecting them, caring for them (as <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 15.6. and 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 5.3.) using them gently, covering their Infirmities.</ns0:note> to the wife, as unto the weaker <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Than the Hus<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bands, and that both in Body and Mind, as Women usually are.</ns0:note> vessel <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">In Scripture any Instrument is called a Vessel, and the Wife is here called so, as being not only an Orna<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment, but an Help to the Husband and Family, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 2.18. This he adds as a reason why the Husband should give Honour to the Wife, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> her being the <ns0:hi>weaker Vessel</ns0:hi>; weak Vessels must be gently handled; the infirmities of Children bespeak their Pardon when they offend; and <ns0:hi>those Members of the Body which we think less honourable, on them we bestow more abundant honour,</ns0:hi> 1 Cor. 12.23. It is a part of that Prudence according to which Men should dwell<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> with their Wives, to have the more regard to them because of their Infirmities (in bearing with them and hiding them) lest they should be discouraged, if they find their weakness makes them contemptible.</ns0:note>, and as being heirs <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Another reason why Hus<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bands should give honour to their Wives, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> Because tho by Nature they are weak and unequal to their Husbands, yet they are equal to them in respect of their being cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led to the same Grace and Glory, there being neither <ns0:hi>Male nor Female</ns0:hi> in Christ, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 3.28.</ns0:note> together of the grace of life, that your prayers be not hindred <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Either, that ye be not diverted and hindred from pray<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing; or, that the efficacy of your Prayers be not hindred, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> by those contentions and differences which are like to arise, if you do not dwell with your own Wives ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cording to Knowledg, and give them the honour that be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />longs to them.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Eternal Life which is the gift of Grace; or, is to be given out of Grace.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 Finally <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 15.5. Phil. 3.16.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>be ye</ns0:hi> all of one mind <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Either be of one mind in the things of Faith; and then this implies the consent of the Understanding; and the next, that of the affections; or, be united both in Faith and Affection, see <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.16. and 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 13.11. and <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 4.2.</ns0:note>, having compassion one of another, <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Mutually affected with each others good or evil, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.15. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 10.34. and 13.3.                   <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>loving to the Brethren.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> love as brethren <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> in Christ; see <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 2.17.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> pitiful <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Ready to shew Mercy, of a merciful disposition, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 4.32. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3.12.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> courteous <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Kind, af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fable, human, of a sweet Conversation, in opposition to sowrness and moroseness. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 23.7. the same word is used.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Prov. 17.13. and 20.22. 1 Thess. 5.18.</ns0:note> Not rendring evil for evil, or railing for railing <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Not recompensing Evil either in Words or Deeds, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 24.29. See on <ns0:hi>chap,</ns0:hi> 2.3. of this Epistle, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.14, 17, 19, 21.</ns0:note>, but contrarywise blessing <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Praying for, and as ye can, doing good to those that do evil to you, or speak evil of you, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.39, 44. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 16.27, 28.</ns0:note>, knowing that ye are thereunto <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Either, 1. To bless those that do Evil to you, that so by patient bearing of Injuries, for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bearing private revenge, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> ye might obtain a Blessing. Or, 2. Ye are called hereunto, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> to inherit a Blessing.</ns0:note> called <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">In your Conversion to the Faith of Christ.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Matth. 25.34.</ns0:note> that ye should inherit <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">This either shews how Believers came to partake of the Blessing, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> by way of Inheritance, Or, it implies the perpe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tuity of it, that whereas they can exercise their Pati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ence in suffering Injuries but a little while, their recom<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pence shall be for ever.</ns0:note> a blessing <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Either, 1. Eternal Life, as the greatest Blessing; or, 2. The good things of both Lives<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Temporal, Spiritual, and Eternal Mercies, which are all promised to the godly, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.8. and which they have by right of inheritance, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 37.11. <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.5. and this seems to agree with <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 10, 11, 12.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:584" />10 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 34.12. &c.</ns0:note> he that will love life <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">He that earnestly desires to lead a quiet and com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fortable Life here, and to enjoy Eternal Life hereafter.</ns0:note>, and see good <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Peaceable, and prosperous; as <ns0:hi>evil days</ns0:hi> are such as are grievous and calamitous, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 47.9.</ns0:note> days, let him refrain his tongue from evil <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">From evil-speaking, railing, reviling, open destruction.</ns0:note>, and his lips that they speak no guile <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Tell no Lies of his Neighbour: Or, this may imply Whispering, Back-biting, or any way, secretly and closely speaking evil of him. Under these two, all the Vices of the Tongue, whereby our Neigh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bour may be wronged, are contained, and the contrary Virtues commanded under the Name of <ns0:hi>Blessing.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 Let him <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 37.27. Isa. 1.16. 3 Joh. 11.</ns0:note> eschew evil and do good <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Let him not only in general avoid all Sin, and exer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cise himself in all well-doing (as the Prophets meaning ci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted in the Margin, seems to be) but particularly, let him avoid all Sin against his Neighbour, not recompencing evil to him, and doing him all the good he can, and over<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />coming evil with good; and to this the Apostle accommo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dates the Prophet's words.</ns0:note>, let him seek peace <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Not only with God, and his own Conscience, but with his Neighbours, which is here especially meant.</ns0:note>, and ensue <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Either seeking and ensuing signify the same thing, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> an earnest desire of Peace, and use of all lawful means to obtain it; or, <ns0:hi>ensuing,</ns0:hi> it may signify the difficulty of obtaining it; when we seek it, it may seem to fly from us, Men may not let us have Peace when we would have Peace, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 120.7. and therefore we must <ns0:hi>follow it,</ns0:hi> Heb. 12.14.</ns0:note> it.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 For the eyes of the Lord <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> over the righteous, and his ears <ns0:hi>are open</ns0:hi> unto their pray<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ers <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">God watcheth over them, looks favouraby on them and hears their Prayers; see <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 34.15. This he lays down as a motive to Patience under injuries, and to keep us from tumultuating Passions, and desires of Revenge; that God sees all we suffer, hath a care of us, and is ready to hear, and in due time to help us.</ns0:note>: but the face <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">His Anger or Indignation; Face being here taken not for God's favour (as many times it is) but in the contrary sence, as <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 17.10. and 20.5. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 68.1, 2. Men shew by their Countenances whether they be angry or pleased; and hence it is that God's Face is sometimes taken for his favour, sometimes for his displeasure. A farther Argument to perswade us to Patience, that God undertakes to plead our cause against our Enemies, and avenge us on them; whereas if we think to secure our selves against them by undue means, we make God an Enemy to us.</ns0:note> of the Lord <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>upon.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> against them that do evil.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 And who <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> he <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> None or few will harm you, as being convinced and overcome by your good Deeds, whereby even they are ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny times mollified and melted that are of themselves most wicked and hard-hearted, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 24.16, 17,</ns0:note> that will harm you, if ye be followers of that which is good <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Either fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowers of God, who doth good to the evil and unkind; but then it should be rendred followers of <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> who is good, or, rather followers of those things that are good, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> if you be diligent in doing good to others, none will have the heart to do you hurt.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 4.14.</ns0:note> But and if ye suffer for righteousness sake <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">If ye suffer unjustly, whether it be for the true Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fession of the Gospel, or in the exercise of righteousness, being followers of that which is good, and walking in the practice of the Duties before mentioned.</ns0:note> happy <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Both in the spiritual benefit ye gain by Sufferings, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> your edification in Faith, Patience, Humility, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> the Glory which redounds to God who supports you under, and carries you through them, and the reward you your selves expect after them, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.10, &c.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>are you,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Isa. 8.12, 13. Jer. 1.8.</ns0:note> be not afraid of their terror <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Either be not afraid after the manner of carnal Men (as the Prophet's meaning is, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 8.) or, ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther (the Apostle accommodating the words of the Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phet to his present purpose) be not afraid of those for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />midable things wherewith they threaten you; or, be not afraid of themselves and their threatnings, whereby they would strike terror into you; and so here is a Metonymy in the words; <ns0:hi>
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ear,</ns0:hi> the effect being put for the cause; thus fear is taken, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 64.1. and 91.5. and <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 1.26.</ns0:note>, neither be troubled <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> inordinately, with such a Fear as is contrary to Faith. and hinders you from doing your Duty, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 14.1.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 But sanctify <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Exalt him in your hearts, and give him the honour of all his glorious Perfections, Power, Wisdom, Goodness, Faithfulness, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> by believing them, and depending upon his Promises for defence and assistance against all the Evils your Enemies may threaten you with.</ns0:note> the Lord God in your hearts, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 119.46. Act. 4.8.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> ready always <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Prepared to answer when duly called to it.</ns0:note> to <ns0:hi>give</ns0:hi> an answer <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>to make an Apology</ns0:hi> or Defence, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> of the Faith ye profess; the word is used <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 22.1. and 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 9.3.</ns0:note> to every man <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Either that hath Authority to examine you, and take an account of your Religion; or, that asks with modesty and a desire to be satisfied, and learn of you.</ns0:note> that asketh you a reason of the hope <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Faith, for which Hope is frequently used in Scripture, which is built upon Faith: The sence is, whereas Unbelievers, your Persecutors especially, may scoff at your hope of future Glory, as vain and groundless, and at your selves, as mad or foolish, for venturing the loss of all in this World, and exposing your selves to so many suffer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ings in expectation of ye know not what uncertainties in the other; do ye therefore be always ready to defend and justify your Faith against all Objectors, and to shew how reasonable your hope of Salvation is, and on how sure a Foundation it is built.</ns0:note> that is in you with meekness and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>reverence.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> fear <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Either with meekness in relati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on to Men, in opposition to Passion and intemperate Zeal (your Confession of the Faith must be with Courage, but yet with a spirit of meekness and modesty) and fear or reverence in relation to God, which, where it prevails, overcomes the fierceness of Men's Spirits, and makes them speak modesty of the things of God, and give due respect to Men; Or, Fear may be set in opposition to Pride, and presumption of a Man's own Wisdom or Strength, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> Make Confession of your Faith humbly, with Fear and Trembling, not in confidence of your own strength, or gifts, or abilities.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 2.12.</ns0:note> Having a good conscience <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">This may be read either, 1. Indicatively, and joined (as by some it is) to the former Verse; and then the sence is, if ye be always ready to answer every one that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you, ye shall have a good Conscience: Or, rather, 2. Imperatively (which our Translation favours) <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> not only be ready to make Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fession of your Faith; but let your Life and Practice be cor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />respondent to it, in keeping your selves pure from Sin, and exercising your selves unto Godliness, from whence a good Conscience proceeds; here therefore the effect is put for the cause, a good Conscience for a good Life, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 23.1.</ns0:note> that whereas they speak evil of you, as of evil-doers, they may be ashamed <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The sence is, that whereas they speak evil of you, as of evil-doers, your good Conversation may bear Witness for you, confute their Calumnies, and make them ashamed, when it appears that their accusations are false, and that they have nothing to charge upon you but your being fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowers of Christ.</ns0:note> that falsely accuse your good conversation in Christ <ns0:note n="*" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> That good Conversation, which ye lead as being in Christ; <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> according to his Doctrine and Example, and by the influence of his Spirit.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 For <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> better, if the will of God be so <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> That ye must suffer; intimating that this is an ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gument for their patience and submission in their Sufferings, and a ground of Comfort to them, that they are led in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to them by the Providence of God (nor by their own folly or rashness) and have him for a Witness and Judg both of their Cause and Deportment.</ns0:note>, that ye suffer for well-doing than for evil-doing.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 For Christ also hath <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 5.6. Heb. 9.26, 28.</ns0:note> once <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">In opposition to the legal Sacrifices which were offer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed from day to day, and from year to year, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 7.27. and 9.25. and 10.12. and this shews, as the perfection of Christ's Sufferings, (in that they needed not be repeated) so our Conformity to him in deliverance from ours; that as Christ underwent Death (the principal part of his Sufferings) not often, but once only, and then his Glory followed; so likewise if in this Life we suffer for righteousness sake, according to Christ's example, there remains no more suf<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fering for us, but we shall be glorified with him, 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 2.12.</ns0:note> suffered for sins <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> For the expiation of Sin. This is another ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gument for Patience under Sufferings, that Christ by his Suf<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ferings hath taken away the guilt, and freed us from the punishment of Sin; so that our Sufferings, though they may be not only by way of Trial, but of Correction; yet are not properly penal or vindictive.</ns0:note>, the just for the unjust <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">And therefore well may we who are in our selves unrighteous, be content to suffer, especially for his Cause and Truth.</ns0:note>, that he might bring us to God <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Recon<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cile us to God, and procure for us access to him with freedom and boldness, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 5.2. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 3.12.</ns0:note>; <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Rom. 1.4. 2 Cor. 13.4.</ns0:note> being put to death in the flesh <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">His humane Nature, frequently in Scripture called <ns0:hi>Flesh,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 4.1. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 1.14. and though his Soul, as being Im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mortal did not die, yet he suffered most grievous Torments in it, and his Body died by the real Separation of his Soul from it.</ns0:note>, but quickned by the Spirit <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> His own Godhead, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 2.19. and 10.17, 18. The former Member of this Sentence speaks of the Subject of his Death, his <ns0:hi>Flesh,</ns0:hi> which was likewise the Subject of his Life in his Resurrection: this latter speaks of the efficient Cause of his Life, his own eternal Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:584" />19 By which <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">By which Spirit mentioned in the end of the former Verse, <ns0:hi>i. e. by,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> his Divine Nature, the same by which he was quickned.</ns0:note> also he <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Christ. This notes the Person that went and preached, as the former doth the Nature in which, and so shews that what is here spoken of the Person of Christ, is to be understood of him according to his Divine Nature.</ns0:note> went <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>came,</ns0:hi> viz. from Heaven, by an Anthropopathy, by which Figure God is often in Scripture said to <ns0:hi>go forth,</ns0:hi> Isa. 26.21. to <ns0:hi>come down, Micha</ns0:hi> 1.3. and <ns0:hi>go down,</ns0:hi> Gen. 18.21. <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 3.8. which two latter places are best understood of the second Person. This therefore here notes in Christ not a change of place, but a special Operation, and Testification of his Presence.</ns0:note> and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 4.6.</ns0:note> preach<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> By <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> inspired by him, that he might be a Preacher of Righteousness to warn a wicked Gene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ration of approaching Judgment, and exhort them to Repen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tance.</ns0:note> unto the spirits <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Souls of Men departed, which are frequently cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led Spirits, <ns0:hi>Eccles.</ns0:hi> 12.7. <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 7.59. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 12.23.</ns0:note> in prison <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In Hell, so it is taken, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 27.20. compare with <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.25. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 12.58. where <ns0:hi>Prison</ns0:hi> is mentioned as a Type, or Representation of Hell; and the <ns0:hi>Syriack</ns0:hi> renders the word by <ns0:hi>Sh<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ol,</ns0:hi> which signifies sometimes the Grave, and sometimes Hell. See the like Expression, 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.4, 5. and <ns0:hi>Iude</ns0:hi> 6.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 7.7. and 8.18.</ns0:note> Which <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Which Spirits in Prison. <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> When were these Spirits, to whom Christ preached by <ns0:hi>Noah,</ns0:hi> in Prison? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> Then when <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> writ this Epistle. The <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> Participle of the Present Tense is here to be supplied, and the word thus read, <ns0:hi>preached to the Spirits,</ns0:hi> which are in <ns0:hi>Prison, viz.</ns0:hi> now at this time; and so the time of their being in Prison, is oppo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed to the time of their being Disobedient; their Disobedi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ence going before their Imprisonment, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> they were diso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bedient then, they are in Prison now.</ns0:note> sometime <ns0:note n="k." place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> In the days of <ns0:hi>Noah,</ns0:hi> when they were upon Earth.</ns0:note> were disobedient <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Would not believe what <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> told them in God's Name, nor be brought to Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pentance by his Preaching.</ns0:note>, when once <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Not always, but for a deter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />minate time, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> 120 years; which term being expired, there was no hope left for them that they should be spared.</ns0:note> the long-suffering of God <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> God in his Patience, and long-suffering.</ns0:note> wait<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">For the Repentance and Reformation of that rebellious Generation.</ns0:note> in the days of Noah <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Till the 120 years were run out, and the Ark, which was a preparing for the Security of him, and his Family, were finished.</ns0:note>, while the ark was a preparing, † wherein few, that is, eight souls <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Eight Persons, <ns0:hi>Noah,</ns0:hi> and his Wife, his three Sons, and their Wives.</ns0:note> were saved by water <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Either, 1. <ns0:hi>by</ns0:hi> Water, is here put for <ns0:hi>in,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 4.11. <ns0:hi>that believe, though they be not circum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cised.</ns0:hi> The same <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> Preposition is used as here, and the words may be read, <ns0:hi>by,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>through,</ns0:hi> or rather <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> Uncircumci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion; for Uncircumcision was not the cause or means of their believing. See the like use of this Particle, 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.5. Thus saved <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> the Water, is as much as notwithstanding the Water, or the Water not hindring; so 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 2.15. saved <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> Child-bearing, where the same Preposition is used: Or, 2. <ns0:hi>by</ns0:hi> Water; the Water, which drowned the World, lifting up the Ark and saving <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> and his Houshold. <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> Doth not this Place countenance the <ns0:hi>Papist</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>Limbus,</ns0:hi> or the place where the Souls of the Old-Testament Fathers were reserved (as they pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tend) till Christ's coming in the Flesh? <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> No: For, 1. The Spirits here mentioned were <ns0:hi>disobedient,</ns0:hi> which cannot be said of the Fathers of the Old-Testament, who were true Believers. 2. The Spirits here mentioned, are not said to be delivered out of Prison, but only that Christ by his Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit preached to them, and to his preaching to them, their dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />obedience is opposed. 3. According to the Papists, <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> and his Family must be in their <ns0:hi>Limbus,</ns0:hi> whereas they are op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posed to those disobedient Spirits to whom Christ is said to preach.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Eph. 5.26.</ns0:note> The like figure <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Gr. the <ns0:hi>Antitype.</ns0:hi> Twice this word occurs in Scripture, once <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 9.24. where it signifies simply a Type, or Exemplar, or Representation; and here, where it implies either the like<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness or correspondence of one Type with another in sig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifying the same thing; so that here may be two types, the Deliverance of <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> and his Houshold in the Flood, and Baptism, whereof the former was a Type of the latter, yet so as both represent the Salvation of the Church in that as the Waters of the Flood li<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ting up the Ark, and saving <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi>'s Family shut up in it, signified the Salvation of the Church: so likewise Baptism signifies the Salvation of those that are in the Church (as in an Ark) from that common Destru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ction which involves the rest of the World: Or, it signifies the Truth it self, as answering the Type or Figure; and thus the temporal Salvation of <ns0:hi>Noah,</ns0:hi> &c. from the Flood, in the Ark, was the Type, and the eternal Salvation of Believers by Baptism, is the Antitype, or Truth figured by it. Our Translation seems to favour the former.</ns0:note> whereunto <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The saving eight Persons by Water, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> the Salvation of Believers now by Baptism, answers to the Deliverance of <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> then; and so this Relative, <ns0:hi>whereunto,</ns0:hi> answers to the fore-going Sen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tence, as its Antecedent,</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> baptism, doth also now save us <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> with an eternal Salvation, in answer to the temporal Deliverance of <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> by Water; and that not only as it is a Sign, but a Seal whereby the Spirit of God confirms in the Hearts of Believers the Faith of their Justification purchased by Christ's Death, and wit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nessed by his Resurrection, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 4.25.</ns0:note>, (not the putting away of the filth of the flesh <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Not meerly the washing of the Body with Water, or the external part of Baptism, which can of it self have no further effect, than other bodily VVashings have, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> to cleanse the Flesh. And so he answers an Objection which might be made, How Baptism can be said to save us, when so many perish who are baptized, by declaring, as follows, what it is in Baptism which is so effectual.</ns0:note>, but the answer <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word here used, is several ways rendred, and so this place differently inter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />preted: The best Translation seems to be, either, 1. the <ns0:hi>Petition</ns0:hi> of a good Conscience, and then it notes the effect of Baptism, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> that holy Confidence and Security where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />with a Conscience, sprinkled with the Blood of Christ, ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dresses it self to God in Prayer, as a Father. Thus the word is taken, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 15.23. and 16.2. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 10.20. Or rather, 2. the <ns0:hi>Stipulation,</ns0:hi> which by a Metonymy is taken for the An<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />swer, Promise, or Restipulation required, and this agrees with our Translation. In Baptism there is a solemn Cove<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nant, or mutual Agreement between God and the Party bap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tized, wherein God offers, applies, and seals his Grace, sti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pulating or requiring the Partie's acceptance of that Grace, and devoting himself to his Service; and when he out of a good Conscience doth engage, and promise this, which is to come up to the terms of Covenant, that may properly be called the <ns0:hi>Answer of a good Conscience.</ns0:hi> It seems to be an Al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lusion to the manner of Baptizing, where the Minister ask'd the Party to be baptized, concerning his Faith in Christ, and he accordingly answered him; <ns0:hi>Dost thou believe? I believe. Dost thou renounce the Devil,</ns0:hi> &c? <ns0:hi>I renounce.</ns0:hi> See <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 8.37.</ns0:note> of a good conscience <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">A Conscience purified by Faith from internal and spiritual Defilements (in opposition to putting away the filth of the Flesh) which only sincerely answers to what God requires in Baptism.</ns0:note> towards God <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In the presence of God, with whom Conscience hath to do in Baptism, and who alone is the Judge of Conscience, and knows whether it be good and sincere, or not: Or, <ns0:hi>toward God,</ns0:hi> is <ns0:hi>to</ns0:hi> God; and then it relates to <ns0:hi>answer,</ns0:hi> and implies the Answer, or Engagement of Conscience to be made to God.</ns0:note>) by the resurrection of Jesus Christ <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Either these words are to be joined to the Verb <ns0:hi>save,</ns0:hi> and the rest of the Verse to be read in a Paren<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thesis, according to our Translation, and then the sense is, That Baptism saves us by the Faith of Christ's Resurrection, or by Virtue derived from Christ's Resurrection, under which is comprehended his Death and Sufferings: or they are to be joyned to <ns0:hi>answer,</ns0:hi> supplying <ns0:hi>which is,</ns0:hi> and then without a Parenthesis, the Text runs thus, <ns0:hi>the Answer of a good Conscience,</ns0:hi> which is, <ns0:hi>by the Resurrection of Christ,</ns0:hi> and the meaning is, That the Answer of a good Conscience toward God, is by the Resurrection of Christ, as the Foundation of our believing the Promise of Forgiveness, and Free-grace, in as much as it testifies God to be fully satisfied for Sin, and Christ to have fully overcome Sin, the Devil, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> For where this Faith is not, there can be no good Conscience, nor any sincere an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />swering what God requires of us in Baptism: If Men do not believe the Satisfaction of Divine Justice by Christ's Death, which is evidenced by his Resurrection, they will not close with the Offers of his Grace, nor engage themselves to be the Lord's. See 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15.17. and this Epistle Chap. 1.3.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22. Who is gone into heaven, and is on the right hand of God, <ns0:note n="*" place="bottom">See <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.34. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 1.3. This is added as another ground of Faith, and a good Conscience,</ns0:note> angels, and authorities, and powers <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">See <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.38. <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 1.20, 21. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 1.16. and 2.10.</ns0:note>, being made <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> by his Father, to whom this subjecting all things to Christ is else<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />where ascribed, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15.27. <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 1.22. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 2.8.</ns0:note> subject unto him.</ns0:p>
